content: Children and infants who have been on first-line antiretroviral therapy (ART) for more than four weeks and weigh at least 3 kg are eligible for dolutegravir (DTG)-based regimens. However, there is limited direct evidence supporting the use of DTG-based regimens in children weighing less than 20 kg when the nucleoside reverse transcriptase inhibitor (NRTI) backbone is only partially active due to resistance to one or both NRTIs. Despite this, programmatic experience has shown effective viral load suppression in children weighing more than 20 kg who transition to DTG-based regimens. Additionally, randomized controlled trials in adults support the use of DTG-based regimens with partially active NRTI backbones. The Paediatric Antiretroviral (ARV) Working Group has provided specific recommendations for both firstand second-line ART regimens. These guidelines encourage the rapid transition to DTG-based regimens for all infants and children older than four weeks and weighing at least 3 kg, regardless of their current ART regimen. The timing of this transition should consider the availability and anticipated supply of DTG dispersible tablets. In cases of limited supply, priority should be given to children who are most in need of DTG, such as those on non-nucleoside reverse transcriptase inhibitor (NNRTI)-based regimens, those requiring tuberculosis (TB) treatment, and those on lopinavir/ritonavir (LPV/r) solid formulations who face challenges with administration or achieving optimal viral load suppression. Viral load testing is not a prerequisite for transitioning to DTG-based regimens, although it remains a good practice for monitoring and providing appropriate care. However, for children on raltegravir (RAL)-based regimens, viral load testing should be conducted before transitioning to DTG. Preferred second-line ART regimens for adults and adolescents include tenofovir disoproxil fumarate (TDF) + lamivudine (3TC) (or emtricitabine [FTC]) + DTG, while alternative regimens may include zidovudine (AZT) + 3TC + atazanavir/ritonavir (ATV/r) or LPV/r. For children and infants, preferred regimens include abacavir (ABC) + 3TC + DTG, with alternatives such as AZT + 3TC + LPV/r or ATV/r. The use of DTG in second-line ART following the failure of TDF + 3TC (or FTC) + efavirenz (EFV) is supported by evidence, but concerns remain about the potential use of suboptimal therapy due to resistance to TDF and 3TC. Resistance to these drugs is common among individuals failing NNRTI-based ART, with up to two-thirds showing resistance to TDF and the majority to 3TC. While DTG appears effective when combined with at least one active NRTI, its efficacy with an NRTI backbone compromised by major resistance mutations is less certain. The DAWNING study demonstrated the effectiveness of DTG-based regimens with at least one active NRTI, but further data are needed to assess its efficacy in cases of extensive NRTI resistance. The NADIA trial in sub-Saharan Africa found that DTG with two NRTIs effectively suppressed viral loads, even in populations with extensive NRTI resistance. This trial also showed that tenofovir could be maintained in second-line therapy without switching to AZT, offering advantages for both users and programs. For third-line ART, WHO recommends regimens that include new drugs with minimal cross-resistance to previously used regimens, such as integrase strand transfer inhibitors (INSTIs) and second-generation NNRTIs and protease inhibitors (PIs). The ACTG A5288 trial demonstrated the effectiveness of regimens containing darunavir/ritonavir (DRV/r) + RAL in achieving viral suppression in individuals with pre-existing LPV/r resistance. Genotypic resistance testing can guide decisions to optimize third-line regimens. Overall, further research is needed to inform the routine use of TDF + 3TC + DTG in second-line regimens, particularly in individuals with resistance to 3TC and TDF. Population-level surveys of HIV drug resistance are also necessary in countries transitioning to DTG to monitor emerging resistance. Additionally, more studies are required to understand sequencing strategies in secondand third-line ART, especially for children and adolescents.
